section.title: Israel Forsakes God
section.sectionRationale: This is the first great oracle of the book's opening movement, the covenant lawsuit proper. Having been commissioned in chapter 1, Jeremiah now brings the LORD's case against His people: a bride's early devotion traded for worthless idols, a fountain forsaken for broken cisterns, and a divorced woman's shameless return to lovers who have already ruined her.
section.thesis: The LORD recalls Israel's bridal devotion in the wilderness, indicts her for forsaking Him, the fountain of living water, for broken cisterns of her own making, and exposes the folly of a people who deny their guilt even as their own history condemns them.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the devotion of Israel's youth remembered; the covenant lawsuit and the forsaken fountain; the relentless chase after other lords; a universal, brazen harlotry; and the searching question, would you now return to Me.

units.label: Remembered devotion
units.note: the love of a bride in the wilderness

verses.text: Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Go and proclaim in the hearing of Jerusalem that this is what the LORD says: 
‘I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.
Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of His harvest. All who devoured her found themselves guilty; disaster came upon them,’” declares the LORD.

units.label: The covenant lawsuit
units.note: the fountain forsaken, broken cisterns dug

verses.text: Hear the word of the LORD, O house of Jacob, and all you families of the house of Israel.

This is what the LORD says: 
“What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me, and followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves?

They did not ask, ‘Where is the LORD who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and pits, a land of drought and darkness, a land where no one travels and no one lives?’
I brought you into a fertile land to eat its fruit and bounty, but you came and defiled My land, and made My inheritance detestable.
The priests did not ask, ‘Where is the LORD?’ The experts in the law no longer knew Me, and the leaders rebelled against Me. The prophets prophesied by Baal and followed useless idols.
Therefore, I will contend with you again, declares the LORD, and I will bring a case against your children's children.
Cross over to the coasts of Cyprus and take a look; send to Kedar and consider carefully; see if there has ever been anything like this:
Has a nation ever changed its gods, though they are no gods at all? Yet My people have exchanged their Glory for useless idols.
Be stunned by this, O heavens; be shocked and utterly appalled,” declares the LORD.

“For My people have committed two evils: 
They have {{azab|forsaken}} Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own {{bor|cisterns}}, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

units.label: Chasing after other lords
units.note: prey, a wild donkey, an unashamed thief

verses.text:
Is Israel a slave? Was he born into slavery? 
Why then has he become prey?
The young lions have roared at him; they have growled with a loud voice. They have laid waste his land; his cities lie in ruins, without inhabitant.
The men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved the crown of your head.

Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God 
when He led you in the way?
Now what will you gain on your way to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? What will you gain on your way to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates?

Your own evil will discipline you; your own apostasies will reprimand you. Consider and realize how evil and bitter it is for you to forsake the LORD your God and to have no fear of Me,” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.

“For long ago you broke your yoke and tore off your chains, 
saying, ‘I will not serve!’ Indeed, on every high hill and under every green tree 
you lay down as a prostitute.
I had planted you like a choice vine from the very best seed. How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?
Although you wash with lye and use an abundance of soap, the stain of your guilt is still before Me,” declares the Lord GOD.
“How can you say, ‘I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals’? Look at your behavior in the valley; acknowledge what you have done. You are a swift young she-camel galloping here and there,

a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, sniffing the wind in the heat of her desire. 
Who can restrain her passion? All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her.

You should have kept your feet from going bare and your throat from being thirsty. But you said, ‘It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, 
and I must go after them.’
As the thief is ashamed when he is caught, so the house of Israel is disgraced. They, their kings, their officials, their priests, and their prophets
say to a tree, ‘You are my father,’ and to a stone, ‘You gave me birth.’ For they have turned their backs to Me and not their faces, yet in the time of trouble they beg, ‘Rise up and save us!’

But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble 
and save you if they can; for your gods are as numerous as your cities, O Judah.
Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me,” declares the LORD.
“I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline. Your own sword has devoured your prophets like a voracious lion.”
Does a maiden forget her jewelry or a bride her wedding sash? Yet My people have forgotten Me for days without number.

How skillfully you pursue love! Even the most immoral of women 
could learn from your ways.

Moreover, your skirts are stained with the blood of the innocent poor, 
though you did not find them breaking in. 
But in spite of all these things

you say, ‘I am innocent. 
Surely His anger will turn from me.’ Behold, I will judge you, because you say, ‘I have not sinned.’
How unstable you are, constantly changing your ways! You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria.
Moreover, you will leave that place with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those you trust; you will not prosper by their help.”

units.label: Can she return?
units.note: the brazen look of a prostitute, yet still His question

verses.text: “If a man divorces his wife and she leaves him to marry another, can he ever return to her? Would not such a land be completely defiled? But you have played the harlot with many lovers, and you would {{shuv|return}} to Me?” declares the LORD.

“Lift up your eyes to the barren heights and see. Is there any place where you have not been violated? You sat beside the highways waiting for your lovers, like a nomad in the desert. You have defiled the land with your prostitution and wickedness.
Therefore the showers have been withheld, and no spring rains have fallen. Yet you have the brazen look of a prostitute; you refuse to be ashamed.
Have you not just called to Me, ‘My Father, You are my friend from youth.
Will He be angry forever? Will He be indignant to the end?’ This you have spoken, but you keep doing all the evil you can.”

azab.gloss: To forsake, abandon, leave behind. It is the covenant word for abandoning a relationship of loyalty and love; Israel's core sin is named here not primarily as breaking rules but as forsaking a Person, the fountain of living water Himself.

bor.gloss: A pit or cistern dug to store rainwater, as opposed to a spring or fountain of flowing water. A broken cistern cannot hold what is poured into it, a vivid picture of every substitute for God that promises life and cannot deliver it.

shuv.gloss: To turn, return, repent. This is Jeremiah's key word for genuine covenant repentance, a physical and relational turning back to the LORD, used with piercing irony here of a people who ask to return without any intention of turning from their evil ways.

basic.context: God calls Jeremiah to remind Jerusalem of an earlier love: how Israel followed Him through the wilderness like a devoted young bride. But that memory only sharpens the charge that follows: God's people have forsaken Him, chased other gods with an appetite Jeremiah compares to a wild animal in heat, and now dare to ask whether God will simply take them back without any real change.
basic.hermeneutics: This is poetic covenant lawsuit language, using marriage and legal courtroom imagery that was familiar in the ancient Near East for describing a broken relationship of loyalty. The hardest thing to sit with honestly is how vivid and unflattering the imagery becomes, God is not softening the charge to spare feelings; the severity of the language matches the seriousness of forsaking the living God for what cannot save.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel's sin is named as azab, forsaking, the covenant word for abandoning a relationship, and specifically forsaking the fountain of living water for broken bor, cisterns, that cannot hold water. By 3:1 the people ask to shuv, return, but Jeremiah's whole book will insist that shuv means an actual turning of life and worship, not merely words.
basic.typology: The forsaken fountain of living water anticipates Jesus' claim to be that very fountain, offering the woman at the well water that becomes in her a spring welling up to eternal life, John 4:14. Where broken cisterns fail every generation, Christ is presented as the fountain that never runs dry and never disappoints.
basic.christ: Jesus directly takes up this image in John 4:10-14 and 7:37-38, presenting Himself as the living water Israel forsook here, the only source that actually satisfies the thirst broken cisterns cannot. Where Israel's history is one of restless searching after substitutes, Christ offers Himself as the end of that search.
basic.god: God is the wounded husband of this covenant, whose anger is not cold rejection but the grief of a real relationship betrayed; He remembers the devotion of Israel's youth even while indicting her present unfaithfulness. His justice names sin honestly, yet His willingness to still ask, in Jeremiah 3, whether she will return shows a mercy that keeps the door open even now.
basic.crossReferences: John 4:10-14 has Jesus offer the living water Israel forsook. John 7:37-38 repeats the invitation publicly at the feast. Hosea 2:14-20 develops the same marriage imagery of a wife pursued despite unfaithfulness. Revelation 21:6 promises the fountain of the water of life freely given at last in the new creation.
basic.oneStory: This is Israel's covenant lawsuit, the diagnosis behind the disaster that will unfold across the rest of Jeremiah: a people who traded the living fountain for cisterns that cannot hold water. The whole story of Scripture answers this failure with Christ, the true and inexhaustible fountain, finally offered freely to all who thirst.

context.literary:
The long oracle is built as a courtroom speech wrapped in a love poem. The Hebrew word for a legal contest, the verb rib, surfaces in 2:9 ('I will contend with you') and again in 2:29 ('Why do you bring a case against Me?'), so the passage opens a case in verse 5, hears the defendant's reply in verses 23 and 35, and returns to the bench at the end of chapter 3. Within that frame the poet moves between three registers. The first is memory, verses 2 and 3. The second is the charge, put as questions, verses 5 to 8, 14 and 17 to 19, 31 to 32. The third is evidence, a rapid sequence of pictures from agriculture and animal life, verses 13 to 28.

The images do not follow one another by logic but by association, each unsettling the one before. A fountain and cisterns give way to a lion's prey, to a slave, to a vine that has gone wild, to a stain no soap will lift, to a she-camel in heat and a wild donkey, to a thief caught red-handed. The effect is of accusation that cannot be answered because it keeps changing its angle. Israel is a bride, a child, a field, a vine, an animal, a criminal, and none of the pictures lets her off.

The questions are the engine. 'What fault?' in verse 5, 'Where is the LORD?' in verses 6 and 8, 'Is Israel a slave?' in verse 14, 'How can you say, I am not defiled?' in verse 23. Almost nothing is told as a plain statement of fact. The speaker wants the listener to answer, and the answers are all damning.

There is also a quiet pivot. Verse 28 turns the gods' own inactivity against them with a taunt: let them rise and save you in your time of trouble. Verse 27 had quoted the same people begging, 'Rise up and save us.' The same verbs are used, one to the God they ignore and one of the gods they cannot make move. The unit closes at 3:5 not with a verdict but with a question about whether the LORD may be asked to take her back, which leads straight into the next oracle.
context.historical:
The speech is usually set early in Josiah's reign, before or near the start of his reform, since it describes pervasive idolatry at the high places and under the green trees, and since it treats Egypt and Assyria as the powers Judah is tempted to flirt with. The addressees are 'the house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel' in 2:4. That language reaches back to the whole covenant people, including the north that Assyria had ended a century earlier, so Jeremiah speaks to Judah with the whole of Israel's history in view.

The agricultural pictures belong to the land. Palestine has no large rivers, and a household depended on cisterns cut into the limestone, plastered and fed by the winter rains. Hairline cracks in the plaster meant that a cistern could slowly bleed away a year's water. A spring, by contrast, ran all year. When Jeremiah sets the spring against the cistern he is describing the difference between security and a household's slow ruin. The rain itself was the point of the dispute with Baal: this was a storm god, supposed to bring fertility, and the quarrel with Israel was over who gave the rain, 3:3 and 5:24.

The political images are just as specific. Judah's courting of Egypt, 2:18 and 2:36, runs through the book, and the Egyptian cities of Memphis and Tahpanhes in verse 16 are named because Egyptian power was both the temptation and the later refuge. Judah's last survivors fled to Tahpanhes after Jerusalem fell, Jeremiah 43:7. The sneer at going to drink the Nile or the Euphrates names the two great rivers behind the two great powers.

The religious scene is a mix. The people still say 'My Father' and expect the LORD to save in trouble, verses 27 and 3:4, while they build altars to Baal. This is not atheism, it is syncretism, the habit of adding gods without giving up the LORD, and the temple, the priests and the prophets are all part of it, 2:8 and 2:26.
context.canonical:
The lawsuit style is rooted in Deuteronomy, where the people were told in advance that heaven and earth would serve as witnesses to the covenant, Deuteronomy 30:19 and 31:28. Here the witnesses are summoned: the heavens are told to be appalled, verse 12. Micah 6:1 to 3 uses the same form and a similar opening question, 'What have I done to you?', and Isaiah 1:2 to 3 also calls heaven and earth as witnesses.

The marriage image runs through the prophets. Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife dramatises the same story, Hosea 1:2 and 3:1 to 3. Ezekiel tells it twice, in chapters 16 and 23, with a bluntness that makes Jeremiah mild. Isaiah answers the accusation with comfort: 'your husband is your Maker', Isaiah 54:5, and names the land 'Hephzibah' and 'Beulah', no longer Forsaken, Isaiah 62:4 and 5. Jeremiah himself returns to the wilderness love of verse 2 in 31:2 and 3, and the fountain of verse 13 comes back in 17:13 with the people of Judah described as those who abandon it.

The firstfruits language of verse 3 draws on Leviticus 23:10, and the claim that anyone who ate of Israel's holy produce was guilty reflects the laws on sacred offerings in Leviticus 22. The wilderness journey recalls Deuteronomy 32:10, where the LORD found Israel in a desert land.

The New Testament takes the water imagery to Jesus. At the well He promises water that becomes a spring in the person who drinks, John 4:10 to 14, and on the last day of the feast He invites anyone thirsty to come, John 7:37 and 38. The Bible's last invitation is the same, Revelation 22:17. The marriage thread comes to Paul, who is jealous that the church be presented as a pure bride to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and to Ephesians 5:25 to 27, where the groom cleanses the bride he has loved.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah's task in these chapters is to make an unbelievable thing believable: that a people with a temple, priests, prophets and the name of the LORD on their lips could in fact have left Him. The first hearers did not think they had. They saw their worship as legitimate, with a little Baal on the side. So the poem refuses to argue the point in theological terms and uses pictures that cannot be dodged. A broken cistern is visible to anyone who has ever relied on one. A she-camel in season is not offended by being named.

The speech is not only prosecution. It opens with the memory of a first love, and that is on purpose: to charge Israel with infidelity, the LORD must first say what He remembers about her. The aim is to stir shame and, beneath it, longing. The question 'What fault did your fathers find in Me?' is meant to open a conversation, and the end of the unit, 3:4 and 3:5, leaves the door visibly ajar.

The unit also corrects a false comfort. Israel assumed that her troubles meant the LORD had failed her, or that other powers were stronger. Jeremiah's reply is that her trouble is her own work, 2:17 and 2:19, and that the cure is not a new alliance but a return. The people were meant to hear that diagnosis and act on it, before the north came.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records the charge God brought against His covenant people at a particular time. Its vivid sexual language describes spiritual unfaithfulness, and readers should not take it as a description of women or as a licence to speak of them harshly. The metaphor is not about gender at all: the LORD is the faithful party, and the unfaithful party is a nation made up of men and women alike, as 2:26 says of kings, officials, priests and prophets.

What carries forward is the diagnosis. The sin is not at root a list of bad acts but a switch of trust, a decision to drink from sources that cannot hold water. Anyone who relies on money, status, a political deal, or a religious routine for what only God can give has done the thing described in verse 13. The passage also warns that a person can say 'I have not sinned', verse 35, and be most guilty at the very point of that claim. What the text does not command is a particular political policy toward Egypt or Assyria, and it is not a rule about which alliances a modern nation may make.

debates.question: Was the wilderness really a time of devotion?

views.label: A deliberate memory of grace
views.case: Verse 2 is the LORD's own account, and He chooses to remember the following, not the failures. Israel did say 'All that the LORD has spoken we will do', Exodus 24:7, and Jeremiah 31:2 says that Israel 'found favor in the wilderness'. The memory is pastoral. It reminds Israel who started the relationship.

views.label: A contrast with the wilderness narratives
views.case: The books of Exodus and Numbers record the golden calf and repeated grumbling, and Ezekiel 20:8 says that the people did not forsake the idols of Egypt even then. On this view Jeremiah's picture is idealised, and the devotion is better described as an early season of promise than as flawless loyalty.

views.label: Both are true on different levels
views.case: Hosea 9:10 holds the two together: the LORD found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, delighting in her, and then, at Baal-peor, she consecrated herself to shame. The first love was real as an event, and it did not last.

debates.bearing: The point is not a historical audit of the wilderness. The LORD is describing how He experienced Israel's early commitment, and how far the people have since drifted from it.

debates.question: Does 3:1 close the door on return, or open it?

views.label: A rhetorical 'no' that shocks by its contrast
views.case: Deuteronomy 24:1 to 4 forbids a man to take back a wife who has married someone else. The BSB reads the end of 3:1 as a question, 'and you would return to Me?', with the implied answer that by every ordinary rule she should not. The surprise is that the LORD later offers the very return the law would refuse, 3:12 and 3:22.

views.label: A direct invitation
views.case: The Hebrew can also be read as an imperative or permission, and older English versions render the end of the verse as 'yet return again to Me'. On this reading the verse sets out the rule only to say that God breaks it in grace.

views.label: A question still left open
views.case: Some readers prefer to leave the final clause as a genuine, unanswered question, so that the offer of the next oracle arrives as an answer, not as something already implied.

debates.bearing: Whichever grammar is chosen, the movement of chapter 3 shows that the LORD overrules the logic of Deuteronomy 24 for His people: the husband who cannot take her back does so anyway, Hosea 3:1 to 3.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 contains a word that is usually God's: chesed, covenant loyalty or loving devotion. The BSB translates it 'devotion'. In most of the Old Testament it describes what the LORD shows His people, Exodus 34:6. Here it is what Israel once showed Him. The reversal is deliberate. The LORD is saying that her loyalty was something He treasured, and that He remembers it as one remembers a gift. The partner word, the 'love as a bride', also belongs to the language of betrothal, a love that had not yet been tested by years.

Verse 3 calls Israel 'holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of His harvest'. Reshit, firstfruits, is the part of the crop that belonged to God by right, Leviticus 23:10. To touch it was to be guilty, and the BSB says 'found themselves guilty' because the verb belongs to the vocabulary of guilt offerings; Leviticus 22:16 speaks of those who eat sacred things and 'bear the punishment for guilt'. Israel is set up as the sacred portion, and her enemies are those who eat what is not theirs.

The sharpest wordplay is in verse 5, which says Israel followed 'worthless idols, and became worthless themselves'. The Hebrew uses hebel, breath or vapour, the word that haunts Ecclesiastes, and the verb of becoming from the same root. They went after a breath and turned into one. One does not simply follow nothing; one becomes like it.

The repeated question in verses 6 and 8 is the Hebrew question word ayyeh, 'where?', which is the root of the question God asks in Genesis 3:9, 'Where are you?' Here it is Israel's guilty failure not to ask 'Where is the LORD?' The three groups named in verse 8 are priests, those who handle the law, and shepherds, whom the BSB calls 'leaders'. 'Shepherds' is the Hebrew word, and when 3:15 promises 'shepherds after My own heart' this is the failed group it has in mind.

In verse 11 the BSB reads 'exchanged their Glory'. The BSB footnote notes the alternative 'their glorious God'. Psalm 106:20 says the same of the golden calf, and Paul quotes the thought of exchange in Romans 1:23. The verb of exchanging belongs to the marketplace, and the people are pictured as making a bad trade.

The 'broken' of 'broken cisterns' translates a participle that means shattered or broken. In 2:21 the LORD asks how a vine of the best stock, the choice red vine that Isaiah 5:2 also uses of Israel, could turn into a degenerate foreign vine. In 3:1 the final clause, as the debate shows, can be read as a question or an invitation; the English translations disagree, and the disagreement is worth keeping in view.

typology.type: The spring and the broken cistern, Jeremiah 2:13
typology.fulfillment: A spring that never fails against a vessel that cannot hold what it is given. Jesus claims to be that source: the water He gives becomes in the drinker 'a spring' of water welling up, John 4:14, and He cries out to the thirsty at the feast, John 7:37 and 38. Revelation ends with the water of life given freely, Revelation 21:6. The type falls short because a physical spring gives only physical relief, while Christ gives life itself, and the invitation is open to the nations.

typology.type: Israel the bride and the LORD the husband, Jeremiah 2:2
typology.fulfillment: The unfaithful bride of Jeremiah finds her fulfilment in a faithful groom. Christ gave Himself up for the church to cleanse and present her without blemish, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and Paul is jealous that the church not be led astray as Eve was, 2 Corinthians 11:2. Revelation shows the bride adorned, Revelation 21:2. The image falls short in one way: Israel's marriage failed on her side, but the church's final union rests on the groom's own cleansing work.

typology.type: The vine planted from the best seed, Jeremiah 2:21
typology.fulfillment: Israel was the choice vine that turned wild, and the failure of the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1 to 7 stands behind it. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine', John 15:1, and claims to be what Israel was meant to be, the one who bears the fruit God wanted. Those who are grafted in remain in Him, John 15:4 and 5. The type is not exhausted by Christ, since the vine also pictures the church as branches who can still be cut off, Romans 11:17 to 22.

study.christ:
The passage never names the Messiah, but it leaves a space only He can fill. The quarrel is over the thing Israel needed and could not produce: a people who would stay. Verse 2 recalls devotion that was real and short, verse 21 records a vine that went wrong, and verse 13 states the problem in its simplest form, the people dug cisterns. The cure the book eventually proposes is not better cisterns. It is a covenant written on hearts, 31:31 to 34, and a righteous Branch, 23:5 and 6, and the New Testament treats both as arrived in Jesus.

Jesus appears almost to answer verse 13 on its own terms. He meets a woman at a well, a place where people draw from a source that must be refilled, and offers water that becomes 'in him' a spring, John 4:14. Later in Jerusalem at the feast of Tabernacles, a festival with its own water ritual, He cries out that whoever believes in Him will have streams of living water flowing from within, John 7:37 and 38. In both scenes the LORD who said 'I am the fountain of living water' is on the other side of the conversation, and the offer is made to people whose broken cisterns are exactly the ones Jeremiah describes: one reputation after another, one husband after another, a religion of mountains and temples.

The marriage thread points the same way. Jeremiah's God is a husband who has been left, and Isaiah promises that He will rejoice over Zion as a bridegroom, Isaiah 62:5. John the Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom, John 3:29, and Jesus Himself speaks of the bridegroom being taken away, Mark 2:19 and 20. Paul calls the church a bride betrothed to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The chain of images means that the God who grieved over His unfaithful wife comes in person to claim and cleanse her.

There is also a more modest point. Jeremiah is a prophet who feels what he says. He weeps over the people, and in the verses that follow this unit his heart breaks with God's. Jesus does likewise: He weeps over Jerusalem and says how often He would have gathered her children, Matthew 23:37 and 38, a sentence that echoes 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number'. The older prophet's grief is the foreshadowing, and the Lord's tears are the fulfilment, because the one who weeps over the city is the same LORD whose cistern-breakers He addresses.

Caution is needed. This chapter should not be turned into a hidden description of the cross in every image. The wild vine does not mean Pilate, and the wild donkey is not a figure of Christ. The link is of theme: a people who cannot hold what God gives, a God who gives Himself, and a Son who is both the source and the one who drinks the cup, Mark 14:36.
study.god:
The most striking thing in this passage is a question the LORD asks about Himself: 'What fault did your fathers find in Me?' Almighty God is willing to be examined. He opens a case, allows a defence, and does not hide behind His office. This is not because He is unsure of the verdict but because the relationship matters to Him. The sovereign Lord takes covenant seriously enough to argue it out in public, and Micah 6:3 has the same posture, 'what have I done to you? Testify against Me.'

The passage shows a God who remembers. The word at the opening is 'I remember', and it is spoken of Israel's youth, not of her sin. His memory is a form of faithfulness: He knows what He has given and what He once received. It is also painful. The language of verse 12, 'be stunned, O heavens, be shocked and utterly appalled', reads like the voice of someone who has not been able to take in what has happened. The Bible does not shrink from saying that the LORD is hurt by unfaithfulness, and that His jealousy is a sign of love and not of insecurity.

Yet He is not only wounded. He is also just. The consequences in the passage are not arbitrary additions: the young lions, the ruined cities, the shaved head in Egypt, verses 15 and 16, are the natural result of what Israel chose. Verse 19 says 'Your own evil will discipline you; your own apostasies will reprimand you.' God's judgment here largely consists of letting the people have what they asked for, the gods that cannot save. At the same time verses 27 and 28 show His irony: when trouble comes they call on Him, and He asks where their gods are.

His attributes interlock. He is the source of life, the 'fountain of living water', a metaphor of sufficiency; He is holy, since Israel is 'holy to the LORD' and anyone who harms her is guilty; He is faithful, since His complaint is that He has kept His side; and He is merciful, since a complaint is not yet a divorce. The last section, 3:1 to 5, should be read slowly. The LORD says that the law would forbid a return, and then in the same breath records Israel's own cry, 'My Father, You are my friend from youth', as if to say that He still hears it.

For worship the passage names what is wrong with a worship that feels like worship but does not trust. The people say 'Rise up and save us' and keep their idols, verse 27. A life that approaches God only in trouble, and elsewhere trusts everything else, is described here as a kind of theft. The corrective is to approach Him as the one from whom everything came, to receive what He gives and to refuse to dig our own cisterns.

crossReferences.note: The LORD found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, a delight, and then she went to Baal-peor and became as detestable as the thing she loved. It is the same story as Jeremiah 2:2 and 2:5 told by an earlier prophet, and it shows that becoming like what you worship is a prophetic theme.

Jeremiah comes back to the fountain image and says that all who abandon the LORD, 'the fountain of living water', will be put to shame and 'written in the dust'. Where 2:13 is the charge, this verse is the sentence, and the dust is the opposite of a spring.

The vineyard planted on a fertile hill that yielded sour grapes is the background to Jeremiah's choice vine turned wild, 2:21. Both passages say that the owner did everything, and both ask the same question: what more could have been done?

Hosea is told to love his unfaithful wife again, and he buys her back. The action shows what Jeremiah 3:1 only asks as a question, that the faithful husband can take back a wife the law would ordinarily keep apart.

The law that says a man may not remarry a woman who has been married to another is the rule Jeremiah quotes in 3:1. Reading the passage shows that the LORD speaks within the covenant framework and then breaks the framework out of grace.

Micah opens another lawsuit with mountains and hills as witnesses and the question, 'What have I done to you?' The structure matches Jeremiah's 'What fault did your fathers find in Me?' and ends with what the LORD requires, not with threat.

The people have not said in their hearts that they should fear the LORD who gives the autumn and spring rains. This shows that the issue behind 2:20 to 28 was the giver of rain, and that the sin of Baal worship was a theft of credit as well as of loyalty.

The wilderness love of 2:2 returns as a promise of restoration: Israel found favour in the wilderness, and the LORD says 'I have loved you with an everlasting love'. The memory of chapter 2 is turned into the ground of the new covenant.

The LORD invites the thirsty to come to the waters and asks why they spend money on what is not bread. It reads like the answer to Jeremiah 2:13, offering the spring freely to the people who tried to dig their own wells.

Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that if she knew the gift of God she would ask, and He would give her living water. The same phrase as Jeremiah 2:13 is now the content of a personal offer, in which Jesus takes the place of the fountain.

Paul describes humanity exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images, using the same exchange language as Jeremiah 2:11. He shows that the Old Testament accusation against Israel is the general condition of the human race.

The last invitation in the Bible is for the thirsty to take the water of life as a free gift. The fountain Israel forsook is finally offered to the whole world, and the offer is as open as it was in Isaiah 55.

study.oneStory:
The story of Genesis 1 to 3 is that humans were made to live from God, and that they chose to live from themselves. Eden is a spring, 'a river watered the garden', Genesis 2:10, and the first sin is a turning from that source to a tree that promised more. Jeremiah 2 tells the same plot at national scale. Israel is brought into a fertile land, 2:7, given a covenant and a holy status, and turns to cisterns of her own. When the poem asks 'Where is the LORD?' it echoes the God who asked 'Where are you?' in Genesis 3:9, and when it says that she forgot Him it names the thing that has happened in every generation since the garden.

The passage also stands where it does in the book as the first full statement of the problem of the people. Chapters 1 and 2 together give a call and a case. The call says why Jeremiah speaks. The case says what he has to say. Everything that follows, the temple sermon, the broken pot, the potter, the scroll, the siege, is an elaboration of what is argued here in miniature: that a people who have left the spring cannot be saved by better cisterns.

The passage looks ahead as well as behind. It prepares for the great reversal of the new covenant, in which the husband who was left says 'I will be their God, and they will be My people', 31:33, and the problem of the heart is dealt with from inside, Ezekiel 36:26 and 27. It points to the water that Jesus gives, which, unlike the cistern, does not run out, John 4:14. And it points to the day when the wilderness love of 2:2 becomes a marriage supper, Revelation 19:7.

In the end, the new creation answers the lawsuit. The Bible's last chapter shows a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1, with the tree of life on either side. The thirst of Jeremiah 2 is not abolished by teaching people to want less. It is satisfied, completely and freely, in the place where the fountain is at last the only source anyone drinks from, and where no one needs to dig a cistern again.

quiz.q: What does God remember about Israel at the start of this oracle?

options.text: The devotion of her youth, her love as a bride following Him through the wilderness.
options.note: Verse 2 opens with this tender memory before the charge of unfaithfulness follows.

options.text: That Israel never once obeyed Him.
options.note: The opening memory is explicitly one of devotion, not perpetual disobedience.

options.text: That Israel built the temple faithfully.
options.note: The passage recalls wilderness devotion, not the later temple building.

options.text: That Israel always trusted foreign alliances.
options.note: Trust in foreign alliances is condemned later in the chapter, not part of the remembered devotion.

quiz.q: What are the two evils God names in Jeremiah 2:13?

options.text: Forsaking the fountain of living water and digging broken cisterns that cannot hold water.
options.note: This is the central indictment of the whole oracle, named explicitly in verse 13.

options.text: Failing to pay tithes and neglecting the Sabbath.
options.note: The two evils named here are forsaking God and pursuing worthless substitutes, not these specific practices.

options.text: Building too many cities and too few farms.
options.note: This is not the concern of the passage at all.

options.text: Trusting priests instead of prophets.
options.note: The passage criticizes priests and prophets alike, but the named evils are forsaking God and broken cisterns.

quiz.q: How does the passage describe Israel's pursuit of other gods?

options.text: Like a wild donkey in heat, whose passion cannot be restrained.
options.note: Verse 24 uses this graphic image to show the restless, uncontrollable nature of Israel's idolatry.

options.text: As a rare and occasional lapse.
options.note: The passage describes persistent, relentless, and shameless pursuit, not rare lapses.

options.text: As something forced upon Israel against her will.
options.note: The text presents Israel as an eager, willing pursuer, not a victim forced into idolatry.

options.text: As a quiet, private matter with no public consequence.
options.note: The passage explicitly ties Israel's idolatry to public disaster and shame, not private, consequence-free behavior.

quiz.q: What ironic question does Israel ask in Jeremiah 3:4-5, and how does God respond to it in the passage?

options.text: She calls God 'My Father, my friend from youth' while still doing all the evil she can.
options.note: The irony is stark: comfortable religious language paired with unchanged behavior.

options.text: She sincerely repents and God immediately restores her.
options.note: The passage shows words without a matching change of life, not genuine repentance.

options.text: She denies knowing God at all.
options.note: She actually claims a relationship with God using familiar language, not denial of knowing Him.

options.text: She asks for a new king instead of God's forgiveness.
options.note: Her words concern her relationship with God directly, not a request for a king.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament pick up the image of the forsaken fountain in Jeremiah 2:13?

options.text: Jesus offers Himself as living water to the woman at the well and to the crowds at the feast.
options.note: John 4:10-14 and 7:37-38 present Christ as the true, unfailing fountain Israel had forsaken.

options.text: It has no connection anywhere in the New Testament.
options.note: Jesus explicitly uses living water imagery that echoes this very passage.

options.text: It is only referenced in the book of Revelation.
options.note: Revelation 21:6 does pick it up, but so do John 4 and John 7, making this an understatement.

options.text: It refers only to literal baptism practices in the early church.
options.note: The imagery is about Christ as the source of spiritual life, not primarily a reference to baptismal practice.

questions: God remembers Israel's early devotion even while indicting her present unfaithfulness. What season of closeness to God do you look back on, and what has changed since then?
The core charge is forsaking the fountain of living water for broken cisterns. What broken cisterns, things that promise life but cannot deliver it, are you still digging?
Israel's pursuit of other gods is described as restless and unrestrained. Where in your life does that same restlessness show up, always chasing the next thing rather than resting in God?
Israel could say, 'My Father, my friend from youth,' while still doing all the evil she could. Where might your own words about God have gotten ahead of any real change in how you live?
Even after naming Israel's guilt so honestly, God still asks whether she will return. What would it look like for you to actually turn back this week, not just to say the words, but to shuv?

translationNotes.note: Living water translates mayim chayyim, water that flows and moves, as opposed to stagnant water collected in a cistern; the contrast between a flowing spring and a static, cracked pit is central to the image.
The valley likely refers to the Valley of Hinnom, associated elsewhere in Jeremiah with child sacrifice to Molech, making this an especially damning accusation rather than a vague reference.

This verse alludes directly to the divorce law of Deuteronomy 24:1-4, which forbade a man from remarrying a wife he had divorced after she had married another; Jeremiah uses that legal background to expose how presumptuous it is for Israel to expect an easy return.
